TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
TUESDAY, 8 NOVEMBER 2022 AT 10.02 AM (AEST)
DAY 9
MR ANGUS SCOTT, Counsel Assisting
MS RENEE BERRY, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR A VIAL, for the Commonwealth

COMMISSIONER: Yes. You are appearing, Mr Scott?
MR SCOTT: I am, Commissioner, with Ms Berry of counsel. I understand Ms Hogan-Doran
has a matter to raise at the outset.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Ms Hogan-Doran, are you on your own today?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: I am this morning, Commissioner. Mr Vial will appear with me this
afternoon. He's presently with the witness, and it's a matter I wish to raise. Just in
relation - the first witness this morning is Mr Scott Britton, who is present. I just wanted to
bring to the Commission's attention, Mr Britton swore his statement on 25 October. Since
that time, in my observation and consistent with my instructions, he has diligently reviewed
additional documents that have been made available to him.
He has also identified from that review a number of documents which we are seeking to
have extracted and produced to the Commission. Despite best efforts, that hasn't been able
to be done before the commencement of his evidence. Mr Britton has obviously been
informed of the content of them and will be in a position to answer questions related to the
subject matter of them. What I have proposed with my learned friend is that following his
evidence, Mr Britton provide a targeted supplementary statement to any issues that require
further material or addressing.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. You puzzle me a bit, though, when you say he can answer questions
relating to the substance of these documents. How are they to be asked if Mr Scott doesn't
have the documents?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: So Mr Britton - I appreciate that, Commissioner. The documents that
he has identified - I do have a list that is available. The difficulty - because there's always a
new difficulty.
COMMISSIONER: It wouldn't be a commission if there weren't.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Indeed. And the pace at which this has moved has been challenging for
witnesses, including Mr Britton. The laptop on which he reviewed those documents has a
time stamp that has confused the date and time order. And so we are having to cross-check
whether the list that was prepared overnight matches the documents that he himself
identified.
COMMISSIONER: Right.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: It's a curiosity. I have had my instructing solicitor confirm the laptop.
We have shown it to my learned friends. It is six hours out. I don't understand how or why
that can be the case, but it appears to have infected the date and time order of some of the
documents that he identified. The statement that Mr Britton prepared is very
comprehensive in and of itself, but he has not had access to all of his protected emails. He
has since had access to some of them. I'm not - and thus I have proposed that he provide a

responsibilities but has taken comprehensive steps within his power to assist the
Commission.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. So supplementary statement, and if we have to get him back, we get
him back, I suppose. Mr Scott, what do you say about all this?
MR SCOTT: I have, in principle, no difficulty with the proposal that there be a supplementary
statement. And it may be that depending on the content of the statement he’s not required,
the statement is sufficient. But we would obviously need to reserve our position until we
have seen the statement.
COMMISSIONER: All right. So resigned to the inevitable?
MR SCOTT: Yes.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: And, Commissioner, as will become plain, Mr Britton - although he had
an important role, he reported to more senior people who I anticipate may be called in
subsequent hearing blocks. Certainly what I had anticipated is that the supplementary
targeted statement would be directed to assisting the Commission to be in a position to
deal with those additional witnesses as they come as well.
COMMISSIONER: Some of them are coming tomorrow, I think.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Not as regards Mr Britton, though.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. All right. Thank you. So, Mr Britton, do you take an oath or an
affirmation?
MR BRITTON: An oath.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
<SCOTT BRITTON, SWORN
<EXAMINATION BY MR SCOTT
MR SCOTT: Mr Britton, you - sorry, Commissioner. Perhaps before I commence with
Mr Britton's evidence, can I hand up a list of the exhibits to be tendered today.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR SCOTT: I understand your associate may have a copy, Commissioner, so it's perhaps
unnecessary.
COMMISSIONER: Right. So we've got - - -

COMMISSIONER: Okay. Right. So do you want to put in Mr Ryman's exhibits ahead of
Mr Britton's? Well, we are going to muck up the numbering unless you do.
MR SCOTT: Yes. Perhaps I should.
COMMISSIONER: Do you have any problem with that, Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Sorry, Commissioner. I was just seeking some instructions on - - -
COMMISSIONER: It's just - - -
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Can we deal with Mr Britton first, perhaps, and then deal with
Mr Ryman when he attends.
COMMISSIONER: I'm just worried about the exhibits, that's all. Can Mr Ryman's exhibits go
in, otherwise we have to adjust everything by a couple of hundred.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: I understand. Those are just documents referred to in his statement.
We are content with that, Commissioner. Just on what will be Exhibit 1173, which is on page
4 of the exhibit list, I'm instructed that the correct document code for this document is
CTH.3510.0002.9576. And that document has been produced.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. I think that's what I have got in my list, although it's got an R. Is the
R a problem?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: It should be an R, yes.
COMMISSIONER: All right. Thank you. Well, I will admit the statement of Mr Ryman, the
notice to produce and the accompanying documents, which will be numbers 1135 through
to 1173, and then Mr Britton's notice to produce and statement, which will be 1174 through
to 1206 as per the schedule.
<EXHIBITS 1135 TO 1206 IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE SCHEDULE
MR SCOTT: Thanks, Commissioner. Mr Britton, you were provided a notice by the
Commission requiring you to provide a statement and produce documents dated 20
October 2022?
MR BRITTON: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And in response to that notice, you produced a statement dated 25 October
2022?
MR BRITTON: Correct.

MR BRITTON: Sorry. Correct. Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. And you produced a number of documents with that statement;
correct?
MR BRITTON: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Is the statement true and correct to the best of your knowledge and belief,
Mr Britton?
MR BRITTON: Yes, it is.
MR SCOTT: Are there any changes that you wish to make to the statement?
MR BRITTON: Not at this point, no.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Have you - since providing that statement and the documents to the
Commission, identified a number of documents that are relevant and responsive to the
notice but which have not yet been produced to the Commission?
MR BRITTON: Sorry, can you repeat?
MR SCOTT: Since providing your statement and the documents to the Commission, have you
had an opportunity to review further documents that may be relevant to the terms of - to
the notice to - - -
MR BRITTON: Yes, yes, I have. As just discussed, I was provided protected emails over the
weekend, as in, the last weekend - I think 5 November was the exact date by which I
obtained those emails, reviewed those emails on the 6th and went through those emails last
night in preparation for this morning.
MR SCOTT: Were you not provided access to your protected emails at the time that you
prepared your statement in the first place?
MR BRITTON: No, I was not.
MR SCOTT: Can you tell us why that was the case?
MR BRITTON: I'm unclear. It wasn't obvious to me that protected emails weren't contained
within the extract. I reviewed the emails - I think there was 9,500 emails to review. I
reviewed each and every one of those emails. It wasn't obvious to me at the time that it
didn't include protected emails. I've subsequently been advised that the protected email
system became available in March 2016. That was from Services Australia over the
weekend. And it was only late last week that I was advised that there would be an additional
extract including protected emails. So I received a device on Friday, that didn't allow me to

COMMISSIONER: Can I just ask: if protected emails became available, did you say, in March
2016, does that mean the earliest of the additional tranche of the emails is March 2016?
MR BRITTON: That's correct, Commissioner, yes. That's my understanding.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR SCOTT: And to what period do the protected emails go up to?
MR BRITTON: For the extract that I received, it was March 2016 through to - there were
emails in there until late February 2017. I ceased working for DHS, that I will probably refer
to by default, but Services Australia on 20 January. I was subsequently cc'd into a number of
emails after my departure. I didn't respond to those emails; it may have just been I was on a
cc list. But, yes, I think it was on or around 20 February 2017.
MR SCOTT: So they go from - - -
MR BRITTON: March.
MR SCOTT: - - - March 2016 to 20 February 2016?
MR BRITTON: '17.
MR SCOTT: '17, I beg your pardon. And how many emails are we talking about?
MR BRITTON: I think the total extract was 83 for that period. And as far as relevant emails,
off the top of my head from last night, I think there's about 30 that may be specifically or
are, or my belief is that they are specifically relevant to the matters of the Commission,
being exchanges in relation to assumptions and costings for NPPs, as well as communication
in preparation for government briefings.
MR SCOTT: And can you assure the Commission that you're in a position to provide a
supplementary statement addressing the relevant emails once they become available to
you?
MR BRITTON: In relation to the protected emails, yes. Yes.
MR SCOTT: Are there any other documents that may be relevant that you've had your
attention drawn to?
MR BRITTON: There are - I have actually had a recent conversation - just better
understanding exactly what the email extracts were, any rules that were applied and other
things. So I'm unclear if there are additional emails relevant to the scope of the
Commission's review. I would need to confirm that.

MR BRITTON: To be honest, I'm unclear how long that would take. It would be dependent
upon the volume and quantum of the emails. The first phase of the review was 9,500
emails. And that was a substantial amount of effort in a short period of time to review every
one of those, and that's reflected within my statement and the chronology. I'm not sure if
there are additional emails. That's the advice I will need to seek.
MR SCOTT: So when you refer to the first effort and the 9,500 emails - - -
MR BRITTON: Yes.
MR SCOTT: - - - that's the first effort at preparing your statement?
MR BRITTON: Correct.
MR SCOTT: 9,500 emails you reviewed?
MR BRITTON: That's right.
MR SCOTT: All right. Do you have any - - -
COMMISSIONER: I'm sorry.
MR SCOTT: Sorry, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: What's the conversation you had and with whom?
MR BRITTON: Sorry, Commissioner?
COMMISSIONER: What was the conversation you had that drew your attention to other
possible emails or - - -
MR BRITTON: We had a conversation last night in relation to the quantum of emails.
COMMISSIONER: Do you mean with the lawyers?
MR BRITTON: Yes, that's correct. Yes, that's correct, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Sorry, Mr Scott. You go on.
MR SCOTT: So are we talking potentially a matter of days, a matter of weeks to complete
this further review?
MR BRITTON: I would be more comfortable to say weeks than days, to be honest, Counsel.
But until - I think I could comfortably provide a supplementary statement in regard to the
83, or the subset of those, within days. If there are additional emails beyond that, I would

MR SCOTT: Okay. Now, just in terms of your period of employment at the Department of
Human Services relevant to this inquiry, am I right in understanding that you were the
National Manager for the Compliance and Risk Branch, Participation, Aged Care and
Integrity Group of that department between 11 January 2010 and 28 November 2016? I'm
taking that from paragraph 9 of your statement.
MR BRITTON: Yes, that's correct. Yes.
MR SCOTT: You mentioned in the initial exchanges earlier that you actually left a little later,
in about February 2017. What position were you in then between November and -
MR BRITTON: So the chronology of events was that I was in that role - in that compliance
role. I think at the time it was called Compliance Risk. There were a number of different
names used throughout that six-year period that I was National Manager. I was seconded to
the NDIA. I think the dates are within my statement, which I can find. But that was
November on or around - within - November 2016. That was initially a secondment until the
end of June 2017. That was a role where I was providing advice to the CEO and the board at
the time around fraud control arrangements and capability uplift.
There was some contact that I recall very early 2017 - sorry, I will go back a step. In
December 2016, where I returned to Services Australia for a period, again, referred to
within my statement. I remained in Services Australia until early January when I returned to
the NDIA to recommence the role that I had within the NDIA. I was involved in subsequent
conversations up until 20 January. So I wasn't in the role of Compliance National Manager. I
was in my NDIA role but providing assistance in that couple of weeks leading up to my final
date, being 20 January 2017. I then, in that period in January, I was working from my NDIA
uilding but still working with DHS colleagues or Services Australia colleagues at the time
before I finally finished on the 20th and then had no further contact subsequent.
MR SCOTT: Okay. So paragraph 12 of your statement, you state that between 2010 and
March 2016 you reported to the General Manager of the Business Integrity Division. Is that
correct?
MR BRITTON: That's correct, yes.
MR SCOTT: And that position was at that time held by someone called Mark Withnell?
MR BRITTON: That's correct.
MR SCOTT: And then from March 2016 until when you left, you reported to someone called
Karen Harfield. Is that correct?
MR BRITTON: That's correct, yes.
MR SCOTT: And she was the General Manager of the Customer Review division?

MR BRITTON: Correct.
MR SCOTT: You refer at paragraph 12 of your statement to the establishment of the
Customer Compliance division?
MR BRITTON: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Are you meaning to refer to the Customer Review division as opposed to the
Customer Compliance division there? In other words, are they the same thing?
MR BRITTON: My recollection was that they were. So I ran the branch, and Karen's division
had the same name. Or Ms Harfield, sorry.
MR SCOTT: And at paragraph 12 of your statement, you state that the establishment of that
division was in response to increasing scale of operations?
MR BRITTON: That was my understanding, yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And what do you mean by increased - or "increasing scale of operations"?
MR BRITTON: Business Integrity division was large, very large at the time, and it had a range
of functions responsible for compliance activities, payment assurance and investigations.
With the build-up of budget measures prior to the date of that division being established,
the responsibilities were considerable under that General Manager. So my understanding
was that with the establishment of those budget measures, the increase in my staffing as
well, within my branch - I think I have referred to it in my statement - at times over 3,000
staff. My understanding was that it was a decision made to create a division to take some of
the pressure off Mr Withnell and also to ensure that we had a single focus on compliance
activities within that division.
MR SCOTT: You mentioned the branch had, at some time, about 3,000 staff?
MR BRITTON: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And in your statement, you mention that at some time it may well have been
one of the largest branches in the Commonwealth?
MR BRITTON: Correct.
MR SCOTT: You referred to the influence of budget measures. What are you referring to
specifically there?
MR BRITTON: Specifically - so these were decisions made by government to increase or
change the way in which fraud and compliance activities were undertaken. So my general
term of budget measures is the process by which New Policy Proposals are considered or
determined by government. Generally, in the space that I'm familiar, being the fraud and

compliance space, that would generally result in additional investment to undertake
additional activities.
MR SCOTT: What sort of activities by that do you mean?
MR BRITTON: So this could be an increase in investigations, or in my space it was an
increase in compliance activity.
MR SCOTT: Okay.
MR BRITTON: More reviews. Yes.
MR SCOTT: Right. So more compliance reviews?
MR BRITTON: Correct. Correct.
MR SCOTT: What are compliance reviews?
MR BRITTON: So compliance reviews - I guess the broader context is that compliance
reviews were generally as a result of the data-matching exercise with key stakeholders,
again, referred to within my statement, but the large majority were the likes of the
Australian Tax Office, Department of Immigration, Births, Deaths and Marriages, and also
allegations or tip-offs from the public. So that's generally the basis by which a review would
be undertaken. Compliance officers would undertake reviews, so they would assess the
information provided within that information matched. They would determine whether or
not there was non-compliance by the relevant customer, and they would make a
determination of eligibility, which often resulted in a debt owing to the Commonwealth.
MR SCOTT: And so the data match, as you are referring to, were matches of data obtained
from various other agencies?
MR BRITTON: That's correct.
MR SCOTT: Including the Australian Taxation Office?
MR BRITTON: That's correct, yes.
MR SCOTT: And would that include PAYG data provided by the Australian Taxation Office?
MR BRITTON: That was one of the data sources received from the ATO. That's correct, yes.
MR SCOTT: What was your understanding of the legal basis upon which the ATO, that is, the
Australian Taxation Office, provided PAYG data?
MR BRITTON: So my recollection was that we had a long-standing relationship with the
Australian Tax Office. That was founded on the initial program, which dates back to the late

that. And then subsequent data obtained through the Tax Office was generally - and it was
my understanding - was generally under agreement, from what I can recall, a formal
agreement. PAYG was one of those data sources that mentioned data-matching program.
We also had tax declaration form data as well, and there may be other sources that I just
can't recall.
MR SCOTT: Yes. So you have mentioned specifically two forms of data, PAYG data and tax
declaration data. So the tax declaration data, what was the basis upon - or the legal basis
upon which that was provided?
MR BRITTON: The exact details I can't recall specifically. I do know that the arrangements
we had with the Tax Office were formal. They were based - as I mentioned previously, they
were based on formal agreement. They were very structured as far as the way by which we
obtained the information we used, stored and applied the information received from the
Tax Office. And that data exchange and those data arrangements are often - from what I can
recall over many years - form the basis of reviews by the Information Commissioner and
others with that role, as well as the likes of the ANAO and the Tax Office themselves as part
of that agreement.
MR SCOTT: So am I right in understanding what you have just said, that you didn't have
personal knowledge of the legal basis upon which tax declaration data was provided by - - -
MR BRITTON: Not that I can recall, no.
MR SCOTT: Okay. What about PAYG data? Did you have personal knowledge of the legal
basis upon which that was provided?
MR BRITTON: I couldn't quote you the specifics as far as what those agreements were. But,
again, just based on my experience and the reflection going through material, I could
certainly see that, again, there was very structured discussions and regular conversations
with the ATO in regard to data arrangements, not only with current state data but also
looking at opportunities to streamline and maximise the benefits of the work that the Tax
Office were doing themselves. They had a number of programs that were focused on
improving data.
MR SCOTT: Can I just refer you to paragraph 52 of your statement on page 9 and ask you to
focus on the last sentence of that paragraph.
MR BRITTON: Yes.
MR SCOTT: You state:
"I had an EL2 employee, Ben Lumley, who was responsible for managing the arrangements
with all data stakeholders, including the ATO, and was an expert in data governance and the
technical elements of data matching."

MR SCOTT: Do you see that? Is he the person we should be speaking to about the legal basis
upon which your department, that is, your then department, the DHS, received PAYG data
from the ATO?
MR BRITTON: He would certainly have more detailed knowledge. Again, not speaking on
behalf of Mr Lumley, but that was his role at the time in the technical elements, and I would
expect also any discussions with ATO direct in relation to any detailed arrangement. Yes.
MR SCOTT: Can I just take to you paragraph 86 of your statement and return to the topic of
the increase in scale of operations of your Department that you describe.
MR BRITTON: Sorry, Counsel. What paragraph was that?
MR SCOTT: 86.
MR BRITTON: 86.
MR SCOTT: You state there:
"My branch was already large and was increasing in scale and complexity. I was experienced
at running large operations and at the time did not consider the additional work by way of
NPPs was unmanageable...”
NPPs, you are referring to new policy proposals?
MR BRITTON: Yes. Yes.
MR SCOTT: And in particular, budget measures involving compliance reviews?
MR BRITTON: Correct. Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you:
"...but I did feel increasing pressure.”
What do you mean by that?
MR BRITTON: I think there were a number of pressures at the time. I think generally, as
referred to in my statement, I had a very large branch. At times, I had 18 direct reports. It
was - I loosely called it a big machine as far as there was a lot of operational activity, a lot of
processing, a lot of staff, a lot of issues. You know, just general day-to-day challenges, given
the volume and quantum. And I mean that in the context of just general management-type
challenges. There was certainly an increasing level of pressure, probably sort of starting in
sort of 2010, 2012, on reflection, where we started to see measures coming through. We
had opportunities to start to look at modernising compliance activity in particular, looking at

improved channels around connection with participants, direct connection using different
channels, and really starting to shift towards a more effective and timely experience.
But that was really overlaid with the fact that we had a number of years, as I'm sure we
would all recall, national emergencies where DHS were the primary lead and responsible
agency for providing emergency response and supports for many citizens that were
affected. That had a direct impact on the work of compliance because many of those staff
over differing periods were realigned to do that work. So that in itself - when there's an
expectation of completing work - that in itself had an impact. But also through this period
where we were being continually asked for the provision of new ideas, new proposals, new
concepts, additional savings, that in itself created additional pressure.
MR SCOTT: By "continually being asked to identify additional savings", in particular what are
you referring to?
MR BRITTON: So this was - these were measures designed to generate savings, so financial
returns for government. But the context for that was that we had a significant volume of
backlog of work, for a whole bunch of reasons. One of those was we simply didn't have
enough capacity to treat the volume of activities coming out of our data matching. But also
the impact of realignment for staff within the agency had an impact. Yes. So I think there
were definitely - we saw a significant shift in the expectation around the generation of
savings. Again, my personal experience is that that's generally the place any government, if
they are seeking savings, they would generally come to fraud and compliance because it is a
mechanism by which savings can be - or funding dollars can be = generated through that
activity.
MR SCOTT: When you say changing - or words to the effect "change in expectation", from
whom were you - - -
MR BRITTON: I certainly felt the pressure internally. I don't know directly where that
pressure was coming from, whether it was all internal or whether it was coming from
Ministers or government. But I think through the initial phase where we brought forward
the concept of PAYG and we exposed the volumes of work that we had been unable to
complete, that in itself created an expectation that then perpetuated through a number of
budget MYEFO and budgets to come back with additional compliance activities that would
generate savings. So definitely the emphasis was on the dollars - the savings associated with
those measures.
MR SCOTT: When you say you felt internal pressure, who are you referring to specifically?
MR BRITTON: Well, you know, for me, it was - you know, I reported directly to Mark
Withnell. We had had a lot of discussions throughout that period around, you know, the
expectation that was being placed on him. So not to put words in Mr Withnell's mouth, but
just on reflection around, "What savings can we generate? What can we bring forward?”
Certainly at the early stages. And then subsequent to that, there were a range of
conversations involving the Deputy Secretary that came to me through Mark Withnell as

MR SCOTT: And who was the Deputy Secretary?
MR BRITTON: At the time, that was Malisa Golightly.
MR SCOTT: Okay. What was the nature of the messages that were passed on to you from
her through Mr Withnell?
MR BRITTON: Well, from Mr Withnell - I don't know what conversations Mr Withnell had
directly with Ms Golightly, but certainly through Mr Withnell it was, "What more do we
have? What can we bring forward?” And I think at that stage as well - I mean, the operating
context at that time was, as others may have spoken to, there was certainly an increasing
expectation from government around the reduction of red tape. So that was a real strategic
driver. And digitisation was a big agenda as well across government. So how do we
modernise compliance systems in particular, but also and importantly, from our perspective
at least - and when I say "ours", certainly from Business Integrity at the time - was around
how do we improve compliance.
There has historically been significant levels of non-compliance within the welfare program
in particular. As I mentioned earlier, we were overwhelmed with work. We couldn't cope
with the volumes. So that in itself created an opportunity to look at whether or not, you
know, we could adopt new processes and practices, whether or not we could implement
new systems and technology to not only streamline our own processes which were
outdated but also improve the customer experience in particular. And I think we had some
early examples of where it was solely and primarily focused on reducing debt, not creating
debt.
MR SCOTT: You referred to significant amounts of non-compliance. What are you referring
to specifically there?
MR BRITTON: So what I'm referring to there is the levels of non-compliance by customers
or - at the time was shown through the volume of data matches where there was a
potential or actual discrepancy between the information provided by the customer or
declared by the customer and the information that was obtained particularly from the Tax
Office or other data sources. But also the levels of error. There were a number of other
programs that were operating within the Department at the time that showed that there
were three, four per cent potential levels of non-compliance. So that's three to four per cent
of outlay. So we are talking billions or potentially billions of dollars.
MR SCOTT: So with reference to the PAYG data matches, why do you use the word
"potential non-compliance" as distinct from actual non-compliance?
MR BRITTON: I think - well, generally my view is that no data matches are a guaranteed
indication of non-compliance. There was always contact and engagement with the customer
to confirm the details or they have the customer confirm the details. So I think that - that's
the reason why I use that term.

MR SCOTT: In other words, it's the concept of non-compliance is subject to further
investigation?
MR BRITTON: Correct. Yes. That's correct, yes.
MR SCOTT: And until further investigation occurs, it's still just a potential as distinct from a
confirmed non-compliance?
MR BRITTON: Yes. That's correct, yes.
MR SCOTT: And from what you are saying, was the issue that there is large amounts
of - there were large amounts of potential non-compliance which the Department didn't
have the capacity to investigate?
MR BRITTON: That's correct, yes.
MR SCOTT: And was - am I understanding your evidence correctly, that you felt under
increased pressure to find ways to somehow investigate those potential non-compliances?
MR BRITTON: I think, yes, I did. And I say, yes, we did. I think there was a general
expectation at that time around recognising the - again, the environment and the context by
which I have provided around the pressures, the inability to complete work, the large
stockpiles of work. There was certainly an expectation around looking at ways by which we
could treat that volume of work.
MR SCOTT: And am I right that if those potential non-compliances could be investigated, an
actual non-compliance is identified, that was potentially a very significant body of funds that
could be recovered to the Commonwealth?
MR BRITTON: That's correct, yes.
MR SCOTT: And hence why it achieved some significance in relation to budget measures?
MR BRITTON: Yes. Yes. I would agree with that statement, yes.
MR SCOTT: And am I understanding your evidence, that it was not uncommon when the
budget was under consideration for your branch to identify means of increasing compliance
activities, to increase savings for the Commonwealth for the purposes of the budget?
MR BRITTON: Yes, yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. I think you mentioned at paragraph 89 of your statement a thing called
the government's budget recovery strategy?
MR BRITTON: Yes.

MR BRITTON: That's a term that was used in conversations, particularly with Mr Withnell.
And I think there was just a general sense around the budget at that time. But certainly
in - that was one of the things that stuck in my mind as far as what was driving or potentially
driving and pushing for additional savings, was statement or comment around, "This forms
part of the government's budget recovery strategy.” Because I think at the time, you know,
the - I can't recall the exact - how many billions it was in total for the number of initiatives
that were brought forward, but it was significant as far as the expected savings associated
with the compliance measures, yes.
MR SCOTT: Just excuse me for a minute. Excuse me, Commissioner. I just had a note passed
to me which I understand is from Senior Counsel assisting the Commonwealth.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, we can fast-track the production of these emails that
